query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Addition of a small amount (~2 at.%) of aluminum during vacuum arc melting of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance at high temperatures by promoting the formation of a continuous, protective alumina scale without degrading its inherent mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in the as-cast condition, exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹), but with poor oxygen resistance due to rapid oxidation.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 2 at.% aluminum into the alloy during vacuum arc melting to achieve a homogeneous distribution within the bulk.
generation.conditions: Exposure at 1000 °C in an air (oxygen-containing) atmosphere for an extended period (e.g., 50 hours) with mechanical testing performed under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous and adherent surface alumina (Al₂O₃) layer that acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the introduced Al preferentially oxidizes to form a protective alumina layer on the surface. This scale slows oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy, thereby limiting internal oxidation and embrittlement. Because the aluminum content is kept low, the overall BCC structure and intrinsic mechanical properties of the alloy are maintained.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated HfNbTaTiZr, the Al-added alloy will exhibit significantly reduced oxidation (e.g., lower weight gain and thinner, more continuous oxide scale) while retaining the ductility (8–16% at room temperature) and yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) of the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated, as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting poor oxygen resistance.
generation.boundary: The Al content must be optimized near 2 at.% to avoid the formation of deleterious Al-rich intermetallic phases that may impair mechanical performance. The protective alumina scale must form continuously on the surface under the prescribed conditions.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimal Al concentration and the kinetics of alumina scale formation on this specific alloy are uncertain. The interplay of the alumina scale with the alloy’s microstructure under prolonged high-temperature exposure may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set with the baseline equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and another set with an added 2 at.% Al via vacuum arc melting. Expose both sets to 1000 °C in air for 50 hours. Following exposure, perform oxidation measurements (e.g., weight gain, oxide scale thickness via SEM/EDS) and tensile tests under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ to evaluate yield strength and ductility.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and continuity (via SEM/EDS)
Tensile testing to determine yield strength and fracture ductility at 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-added alloy does not show a significantly lower oxidation rate (e.g., similar weight gain and oxide scale characteristics as the untreated sample) or if its mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) are significantly degraded compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is rejected.
